1:
Two of them stop at the bare fact that an age is given. Clarke calls it worthy of remark that Sarah is the only woman in the sacred writings whose age, death and burial are distinctly noted, and adds that she was deemed worthy of higher honour, Paul making her a type of the Church and her faith in the promise of a son being celebrated among the examples of faith. Ellicott notes the same singularity and assigns the reason, that the honour was hers as ancestress of the Hebrew race. Both draw the arithmetical inference, that since she was ninety at Isaac's birth he must now be thirty-seven; Gill reports that the chapter's placing after the offering of Isaac led many Jewish writers to fix his age at the binding by that reckoning, thirty-seven. Henry takes the number differently, noticing that Sarah had called herself old forty years before, and drawing the moral that old people die never the sooner but may die the better for reckoning themselves old — the longest liver must die at last, and the special friends and favourites of Heaven are not exempted.

Calvin alone attends to the Hebrew, which repeats the word for years after each numeral, and uses it to dismiss a piece of rabbinic ingenuity. The repetition, some had said, means Sarah was as beautiful at a hundred as at twenty and as modest in the flower of her age as at seven; Calvin answers that this is their custom, inventing frivolous trifles to prove themselves skilful at honouring their nation, and betraying a shameful ignorance of their own language, where such repetition is usual. The place-name draws the same kind of contest. Gill reports Jarchi's two, that the name came either from four Anakim who lived there or from four couples buried there — Adam and Eve, Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, Jacob and Leah — noting the second must be by anticipation, and prefers Aben Ezra's, that it came from Arba, a great man among them. Clarke settles on a Canaanite chief with three brothers. Ellicott takes the literal City of Four with the meaning of Hebron, alliance, and suggests a town founded by a union of four families, Arba becoming a personal name from the city rather than the reverse. Calvin declines to choose, suspending judgment on a matter not necessary to be known.

The word came needs explaining, and Calvin reasons it out. If both had merely changed abode the wording would not stand, since Moses says Abraham came to bury his dead; he was not present when she died. Nor will it do to suppose them separated only by different tents, as though he walked twenty paces to mourn. Some suspect a journey; Calvin thinks it likelier their dwelling was at Hebron or the vale of Mamre. Clarke answers practically: Abraham had settled at Beersheba, twenty-four miles off, and for his flocks kept several temporary residences, so his coming means travelling from one to another on the news of her death. Ellicott agrees, guessing that Isaac had been left at Hebron in charge of his mother and the cattle. On the mourning Henry and Wesley say the same thing in the same words: Abraham did not merely perform the customary ceremonies but sincerely lamented, hence the two verbs, to mourn and to weep. Henry presses further, picturing him sitting by the body that his eye might affect his heart, and arguing that lamenting our near relations is a duty and not merely lawful, tears being a tribute due to our friends — when a body is sown it must be watered — though we are not to sorrow as those without hope. Keil and Delitzsch look past the grief to the next move: Abraham rose from before his dead and went to the Hittites, lords and possessors of the city, to procure a burying-place.
3:
Calvin notices what the narrative omits and what it dwells on: Moses says nothing of the burial rite, yet recites the purchase of the sepulchre at great length. That leads him to the custom itself, observed religiously in all ages and among all peoples, ceremonies differing and men outdoing one another in superstition, but burial common to all. It arose not from foolish curiosity or fruitless consolation or superstition, but from the natural sense God imbued men with and never suffered to perish, that they might be witnesses to themselves of a future life; and those who circulate outrageous sayings in contempt of burial cannot, he says, have spoken from the heart. Gill and Clarke explain the standing up literally: Abraham had sat on the ground some days in token of sorrow, as the custom was, and rose when that time was over to see to the funeral. Ellicott orders the two acts: his first care on reaching Hebron was to prostrate himself in Sarah's tent and give utterance to grief, and only after that does he rise.

Henry turns the same movement into counsel. Those in danger of over-grieving must take heed of poring on the loss and sitting alone and melancholy; there must be a time of standing up from before the dead and ceasing to mourn, since our happiness is not bound up in the life of any creature, and the care of a funeral may divert grief where it is likeliest to tyrannise. Weeping, he says, must not hinder sowing. Henry also finds it strange that Abraham should have this to do only now, imputing it to God's providence rather than any improvidence of his, since God gave him no inheritance in Canaan — and adds that it were well if all who provide burying-places for their bodies were as careful to provide a resting-place for their souls. Wesley draws his own conclusion from burying the dead out of sight: death will make those unpleasant to our sight who while they lived were the desire of our eyes, the countenance once fresh and lively becoming pale and fit for the land of darkness.

The self-description as stranger and sojourner is read two ways. Clarke takes the epistles as proof that the words concern Abraham's mind rather than his circumstances, since he felt he had no certain dwelling place and sought by faith a city with foundations; and he notes that in various nations burial in another man's ground was reckoned ignominious, which may be why the offered sepulchres are declined and a purchase pressed. Ellicott supplies the legal position: strangers might pasture cattle on the open downs, but permanent occupation needed the natives' consent, and appropriation required a public compact ratified by the whole tribe at the gate. Calvin offers two readings, either that Abraham makes his suit likelier to succeed by asking humbly, or that he forestalls suspicion of covetousness — I do not desire your possessions, that I may hereafter contend for equality with you; it is enough to have a place where we may be buried. The answering title draws a note on Hebrew idiom, since a prince of God means a prince of surpassing excellence, as Ellicott illustrates from the wind of God, the cedars of God, and a sleep of Jehovah for a deep sleep. Calvin sees a seed of piety in the Hittites for honouring gifts they knew to be God's, and turns it on the reader: if men defiled with so many vices could do that, what excuse have we who give no honour to the image of God when it shines before our eyes? Ellicott adds the commercial reality: the courteous offer never meant a free sepulchre, the payment kept in the background in Oriental fashion but presupposed on both sides. Wesley marks the contrast of titles: Abraham called himself a stranger, they call him a great prince.
7:
Why Abraham refuses a free grave is Calvin's question, and he rejects the obvious answer. Some suppose he declined the favour so as not to be obliged in so small a matter; Calvin thinks he wished rather to show that he would receive no gratuitous possession from men who were to be ejected by the hand of God so that he might succeed them, keeping his thoughts so fixed on God that he preferred the bare promise to present dominion over the land. Calvin also pauses on the gesture, noting that Moses commends the holy man's modesty in rising to bow to the people, and that the word means simply the reverence a man declares by bending the knee or some other gesture — paid to men as well as to God, though for a different end, since men bow to one another for civil honour. Gill explains the posture before it: Abraham had sat down after his speech to await an answer, or was made to sit by men who reverenced so great a personage, and rose when they had done. Wesley draws the whole into a maxim: religion teaches good manners, and those abuse it who place it in rudeness and clownishness.

The name of the cave means double, and the corpus divides gently over what was doubled. Ellicott takes it for an outer and an inner compartment, and reports that because the surrounding land is also called the field of Machpelah some have imagined the valley was the double thing, though he thinks the name more probably came from the cavern. Calvin canvasses a version in which one part lay above and the other below, prefers a single entrance with the cave divided within by a middle partition, and then leaves it open, allowing everyone to adopt what opinion he pleases. Clarke reconstructs the staging of the negotiation. Abraham had already seen the cave and field and found out whose they were, and came to the gate of Hebron, where the elders sat to administer justice and where bargains were made and witnessed; there he addressed the elders, among whom Ephron was sitting, though apparently unknown to him personally, and asked them to use their influence with the owner. Ellicott corrects the English at this point, since the text does not say Ephron dwelt among the Hittites but that he was sitting in their midst, every free-born citizen having a right to be present at such assemblies, where matters were settled by common consent.

Ellicott finds a second mistranslation in the same request and thinks it serious. The English has Abraham asking a burying-place among the Hittites, which he calls quite wrong: Abraham had no wish that Sarah lie among them; the Hebrew asks that the cave be given him in the midst of them, in a general assembly, so that the sale be duly attested. He then catches the tone of Ephron's answer, where the field is thrice said to be given: the same courtly idea as in the earlier offer, that the parties were not buying and selling but making mutual presents. Wesley notices the speed of it: Abraham expected to entreat for a sale and got an outright gift at the first mention; Gill adds that the refusal was not of the request but of the payment. Calvin turns the insistence on paying into a rebuke of ordinary dealing: by offering a full price Abraham cultivated equity, where scarcely a man does not in buying pursue his own advantage at another's cost — the seller setting the price at twice the worth and the buyer shuffling to bring it low, so that there is no end of bargaining. Calvin adds the rule Abraham kept about gifts, having been presented with much by the kings of Egypt and Gerar: that he would neither receive all, nor in all things, nor from all men.
12:
Abraham bows a second time, and Ellicott reads the gesture as the Oriental way of returning thanks for a request granted, the same courtesy as at verse seven; the next step, he says, is to fix the price. Gill takes it rather as a bid for the floor, great respect paid to Ephron and to the assembly, and a signal that he had something to say and desired audience of them. What he says is a refusal, and Clarke thinks our version obscures it: for "if thou wilt give it" we should read "but if thou wilt sell it," and the keseph Abraham offers is silver, not coined money, for it is not probable that any such was then in use. Ellicott finds the Hebrew barer still, no verb of giving at all but simply "but if thou wilt, I pray thee, hear me," a strong desire that Ephron listen to the next request. Wesley defends the refusal on two grounds and neither is pride. It was justice: Abraham was rich in silver and gold and would not take advantage of Ephron's generosity. It was also prudence: he would pay for the field lest Ephron, when the good humour was over, should upbraid him with it.

Henry makes the openness of the transaction its lesson: prudence as well as justice directs us to be fair and open in our dealings, and cheating bargains will not bear the light. Although all Canaan was Abraham's by promise, he notes, the time of possessing it was not come, so what he had occasion for he bought and paid for — dominion is not founded in grace, and the saints' title to an eternal inheritance neither entitles them to the possessions of this world nor justifies them in doing wrong. Ephron names his figure, and the two who price it disagree. Clarke observes that "is worth" is not in the text but must be supplied for our idiom, and reckons the shekel, following Dr. Prideaux rather than the general opinion of two shillings and sixpence, at three shillings English, making four hundred of them sixty pounds sterling; he insists a weight is meant, not a coin, since the next verse says Abraham weighed the silver. Ellicott puts the sum at about fifty pounds, no mean price considering the high value of silver in those days, and adds that our version misses the courtliness: Ephron fixes the price only indirectly, asking what four hundred shekels is betwixt him and Abraham.

Gill says Abraham closed at once, judging it a moderate price between man and man. On the silver being current with the merchant, Clarke glosses ober lassocher as passing with the traveler, the sort used by those who carried merchandise about, what we should call a hawker or peddler. Ellicott presses the point further: shekel means weight, coinage came long afterwards, and by inserting the word money our version antedates the facts, for the Hebrew makes it the silver that was current with the merchants — metal probably drawn into small bars and marked by the refiner to indicate quality, of which Abraham weighed out some two hundred ounces. Calvin spends his comment demolishing Jerome, who had said a letter was dropped from Ephron's name once he consented to take money, his virtue being maimed by the sale of a sepulchre. The name is written exactly as before, Calvin answers; nor is it a fault that a man pressed to sell took the lawful price for his estate, and if there was any sin here Abraham must bear the whole blame. From Jerome's remark the Canonists made it sacrilege to sell sepulchres, while the papal clergy suffer no grave to be dug unless the price be paid.
17:
The deed itself settles one dispute. Gill points out that a field is said to be in Machpelah, and a field could never be said to be in a cave; so Machpelah is the proper name of a tract of ground and not an appellative, whatever the double cave may mean. He notes that some have been stupid enough, as Vatablus observes, to render it "the field of Ephron, which was in the double cave," and that the Vulgate at least inverts this to better sense, though not agreeably to the Hebrew. Clarke adds only that the trees standing in the field were possibly all specified in the agreement. Ellicott takes "before Mamre" as opposite to it, and works out the topography: the Haram where the bodies of Abraham and Sarah lie is on the eastern side of the valley, so the oak-grove must have stood on its western slope. The old Christian tradition putting it at Ramet-el-Chalil neither fits that description nor is near enough, and the remains shown there as Abraham's house are the ruins of a heathen temple. He thinks it useless in any case to hunt for the remains of a nomad who lived in tents, especially where a great city has since stood.

Ellicott adds that Hebron has itself moved, citing Benjamin of Tudela, who nearly seven centuries ago found the old city abandoned on the heights and the new one lying in the valley. What interests him most is the character of the record: he finds it worth comparing this document, so legally exact and full, with the terra-cotta tablets now in our museums which register with equal exactness the daily business of the people of Ur-Chasdim, the very city Abraham had left. Keil and Delitzsch read the same exactness theologically. The narrative repeats, with what he calls legal accuracy, that the field and its cave were conveyed to Abraham for a burial-place, and that repetition measures how much the event mattered to the patriarch: to purchase a burying-place in strictly legal form, as an hereditary possession in the promised land, was a proof of his strong faith in the promises of God and their eventual fulfilment. He traces the grave forward through the family — Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah laid there, Leah buried there by Jacob, and Jacob himself asking to be brought to it. Gill says more plainly that it was to be enjoyed by Abraham and his for ever as his own property, because purchased by his own money.

Clarke calls this the earliest account on record of the purchase of land, and cannot admire enough the simplicity and candour on both sides: the gate where justice was administered and bargains concluded, the offer of a free sepulchre out of common hospitality, the refusal, the silver weighed down, and the passers-by going out to their work in the country serving as witnesses. The conveyance was thus made sure, he says, without the intervention of those puzzlers of civil affairs by whose chicanery property becomes insecure — a censure he immediately qualifies, since it does not touch lawyers properly so called, who are men of honour, but the accumulation and complexity of modern systems of law. Gill sees the burial itself as part of the security, Sarah's interment being possession taken for the use the ground was bought for, and a pledge and earnest of the land promised to Abraham's seed. He and Ellicott both pause over Stephen's speech, which appears to confuse this purchase with another; Gill answers from the wording, that Abraham had a possession to bury in but not to live upon, no ground of his own to till or sow or build on. Wesley leaves the plain remark: those that have least of this earth find a grave in it.
